new_statements.quote: 147. Orhon Türkçesinde sözcük vurgusu, belirli istisnalar dışında, genellikle son hece üzerinde idi. Ünlü nöbetleşme ve değişmelerinin genellikle son hece dışındaki hecelerde olması bu görüşü destekler [...] Üç heceli sözcüklerde, ilk hecede de ikinci derecede bir soluk vurgusu vardı; orta hece ise vurgusuzdu. Bu nedenledir ki orta hecenin kısa dar ünlüsü zayıftı ve birçok durumda düşüyordu: adrıl- < *adırıl-, vb. Eklenmede sözcük vurgusu son heceye kayıyordu: bodun "halk", bodunum "halkım", bodunumın "halkımı", vb. Ancak, belirli ekler vurguyu üzerlerine çekmiyor, vurgu ekten önceki hece üzerinde kalıyordu: bérmädi "vermedi", udımatı "uyumayarak", kılınmadok "yaratılmamış", biliŋ "bilin!", anın "onun ile", okun "ok ile", kaganımın "hakanımla birlikte", otça "ateş gibi", vb.
new_statements.translation: 147. In Orkhon Turkic, word stress was, apart from certain exceptions, generally on the last syllable. That vowel alternations and changes generally occur in syllables other than the last supports this view [...] In trisyllabic words there was also a secondary (breath) stress on the first syllable; the middle syllable was unstressed. This is why the short high vowel of the middle syllable was weak and in many cases dropped: adrıl- < *adırıl-, etc. Under suffixation the word stress shifted to the last syllable: bodun 'people', bodunum 'my people', bodunumın 'my people (acc.)', etc. However, certain suffixes did not attract the stress; the stress stayed on the syllable preceding the suffix: bérmädi 'did not give', udımatı 'without sleeping', kılınmadok 'not created', biliŋ 'know!', anın 'with it', okun 'with an arrow', kaganımın 'together with my kagan', otça 'like fire', etc.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (273 pp. The quoted par. 147 'Vurgu' is at the stated locator: printed pp. 78-79 = pp. 79-80 ( lines 4173-4197; extracted text). I rendered pp. 79-80 to PNG (110 dpi full page, 300 dpi crops) and read the passage on the page scan: the Turkish text in the report matches word for word, from '147. Orhon Türkçesinde sözcük vurgusu, belirli istisnalar dışında, genellikle son hece üzerinde idi' through 'ótça "ateş gibi", vb.' The only differences are the acute stress marks Tekin prints on the example words, which the scanned drops and the compiler disclosed: printed forms are alpagú ~ yılpagút, ärsä́r ~ irsä́r, adrı́l- < *adırıl-, bodún, bodunúm, bodunumín, bírmädi, udímatı, kılínmadok, bí…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the final syllable of the word, shifting rightward onto each added suffix, except that certain suffixes (verbal negative -mA-, imperative 2pl -(X)ŋ, instrumental +(X)n, equative +čA) are pre-stressing: stress stays on the syllable before them. Trisyllables carry a secondary stress on the first syllable and an unstressed (syncope-prone) middle syllable. Erdal 2004 (p. 98) states the same default independently and adds first-syllable stress for expressive reduplicated adjectives, the pronominal stem ka+ and probably adverbs, but stresses (p. 242) that 'we know nothing certain about stress in Old Turkic': the rule is reconstructed from syncope patterns and by analogy with modern Turkic.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Tekin 2003 p. 78: in trisyllabic words a secondary ('ikinci derecede bir soluk vurgusu') stress on the first syllable; middle syllable unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Pre-stressing suffixes: negative -mA- (bérmädi, udımatı, kılınmadok), imperative -(X)ŋ (biliŋ), instrumental +(X)n (anın, okun, kaganımın), equative +čA (otça) (Tekin 2003 p. 79). Erdal 2004 p. 98: first-syllable stress with expressive adjective reduplication and the pronominal stem ka+ (p. 215: kaltï < ka+la+tï by syncope 'due to strong accent on the first syllable'); adverbs possibly initial-stressed; instrumental/equative suffixes possibly unstressed; p. 242: aorist negative -mAz stressed vs. other -mA- forms pre-stressing; p. 427 postposed personal pronouns presumably unstressed; p. 525 interrogative/particle emi-type words with initial stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (sözcük vurgusu), inflected word including suffixes; Tekin's statement is specifically about Orkhon Turkic (8th-c. runic inscriptions), Erdal's about Old Turkic generally (Orkhon, Uyghur, Qarakhanid). Both are reconstructions for a dead language inferred from syncope/vowel-alternation patterns plus comparison with modern Turkic, not observed stress.
new_statements.identity_note: oldt1247 'Old Turkish' is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid (ISO 639-3 otk, Old Turkish) with zero descriptive refs attached; Glottolog 5.1 files all the Old Turkic grammars (Erdal 2004, Tekin 1965/1968/2003, Gabain 1950, Kononov 1980, Johanson 2021 'East Old Turkic', Nasilov 1960, Kondrat'ev 1981) under language code 'Old Turkic = Old Turkish = Old Uighur [oui]' = Old Uighur, glottocode oldu1238. The quoted statement (Tekin 2003) describes Orkhon Turkic, the 8th-century runic-inscription variety; Erdal 2004 covers Old Turkic as a whole (Orkhon runic, Old Uyghur, Qarakhanid). Any catalog entry should be keyed to Old Turkic/otk with a pointer to oldu1238 to avoid double-counting.

new_statements.quote: 2.3. Stress. In Orkhon Turkic the accent probably was an expiratory stress and fell upon the last syllable in general. The fact that the vowel alternations and changes generally take place in non-final syllables testifies to this assumption [...] In trisyllabic words a secondary stress probably fell upon the first syllable. The medial syllable was obviously unstressed. For this reason its short narrow vowel was extremely reduced and subject to fall in many cases [...] When a suffix was added to a word, the stress shifted upon the latter: [bodun, bodunum, bodunumin] Certain suffixes, however, did not take the stress; [birmädi, biliŋ, oqun, qaγanïmïn, otča; scanned-normalized]

new_statements.relation_note: No catalog record (in_catalog false). The one statement held by the project (Tekin 2003 par. 147, fixed: final syllable, secondary stress on first syllable of trisyllables, stress shifts to suffixes, certain suffixes unstressed) is the author's Turkish rewriting of exactly this 1968 section; the 1968 English original says the same, sentence for sentence (2003 adds more unstressable-suffix examples: udïmatï, kïlïnmaduk, anïn). Same placement and type -> agrees; it confirms the compilers inference about the 1968 edition.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent in Orkhon Turkic was (probably) an expiratory stress on the last syllable of the word; when suffixes are added the stress moves to the new final syllable; a closed set of suffixes (examples: negative -ma-, 2pl imperative -(X)ŋ, instrumental -(X)n, equative -ča) do not take the stress, which then stays on the syllable before them. Evidence cited: vowel alternations/reductions occur in non-final syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In trisyllabic words a secondary stress 'probably fell upon the first syllable'; the medial syllable was unstressed and its short narrow vowel reduced/syncopated (2.1711.1: adrïl- < *adïrïl- etc.).
new_statements.exceptions: 'Certain suffixes, however, did not take the stress': examples birmädi 'he did not give' (negative), biliŋ 'know ye!' (imperative), oqun 'with an arrow' and qaγanïmïn 'with my kagan' (instrumental), otča 'like a fire' (equative), printed with the accent mark on the pre-suffix syllable. The whole statement is hedged 'probably' (stress is reconstructed; the script does not mark it).
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Orkhon Turkic, the language of the five 8th-century runiform inscriptions (Kül Tigin, Bilgä Kagan, Tonyukuk, Ongin, Küli Čor), with Uigur/Yenisei/Irq Bitig material cited only for comparison; Glottolog files these grammars under Old Turkic oldu1238, of which the bookkeeping code oldt1247 'Old Turkish' is a doublet (mirror identity note). Stress is reconstructed ('probably'), since the script does not mark it.

readall_conflicts: No new source was opened, so there is no new disagreement to report. 147 states that Orkhon Turkic word stress was generally on the final syllable, with certain exceptions (some suffixes such as negative -mA-, converb -mAtI(n), -mAdOk, imperative -(X)ŋ, instrumental +(X)n, equative +čA do not take stress; stress shifts rightward under suffixation; a secondary breath stress on the first syllable of trisyllables, medial syllable unstressed). Erdal 2004 sec. 2.403 pp. 97-99 is more cautious: syncopation of medial vowels 'should mean that the first and the last syllable of a word had some prominence over the others, or that medial vowels were not stressed', and he 'would assume that Old Turkic stress was not much different from that of modern languages: default stress on the word's last syllable', with first-syllable stress in reduplicated adjectives, the pronominal stem ka+, pre-stressed -mA-, and possibly adverbs and instrumental/equative forms. The two agree on default final stress; Erdal frames it as an assumption from syncopation patterns and the modern languages rather than a demonstrated fact, and neither describes it as a firm phonological rule since the runic and Uyghur scripts do not mark stress.

sources.note: Explicit section 'Vurgu' par. 147, pp. 78-79: word stress in Orkhon Turkic was, with certain exceptions, generally on the last syllable; trisyllables had a secondary stress on the first syllable and an unstressed middle syllable (hence medial syncope adrıl- < *adırıl-); stress moves to the final syllable under suffixation (bodun, bodunum, bodunumın); certain suffixes (negative -mA-, imperative -(X)ŋ, instrumental +(X)n, equative +čA) do not take stress, which stays on the preceding syllable.

sources.note: scanned text a full-text search for stress/accent/stress: comparative statement only — Common Altaic root-syllable (prima) stress, later ultima accentuation in Turkic; alliteration in Uyghur folk songs taken as evidence that prima accentuation 'may well have survived in Turkic down to historical times'; modern Turkic final stress with enclitic exceptions (equative, negative -ma-). No Old Turkic-specific rule.
